title: Niroshan Benjamin
text: My name is Niroshan, and I’m from Vancouver. I completed my undergraduate studies at SFU with a combined major in computing science and business. Towards the end of my degree, I started taking more data science courses, which were very interesting, so I decided to pursue the MDS program at UBC. I hope to eventually work as a product data scientist at Microsoft because I loved the office when I visited for a hackathon.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
On the first day of orientation, I was very excited as I met a few people who wanted to join the UBC basketball intramurals and also met somebody I knew from SFU. For the rest of the orientation, they explain how quizzes weren’t in the class, and if you receive 3 C letter grades, you are removed from the program, which slightly worried me.
When classes started, I was surprised by the number of people on campus even though classes didn’t officially start. I was also extremely surprised by the number of assignments we need to complete in one week and the time we spend on each one.
I feel I can manage the workload, but I am more worried about the quizzes, especially in the statistics class, and the content was hard for me.

title: Penguins Data R Analysis
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. The data ships with the palmerpenguins R package under a CC0 licence.
Cited as the package asks: Horst AM, Hill AP, Gorman KB (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data. R package version 0.1.0. https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/. doi: 10.5281/zenodo.3960218.
The ggplot code in this post is adapted from work I did in DSCI 523 Lab 2, where the plotting template was provided as part of the lab.
Two of the penguins are missing their bill and body mass measurements, so they are dropped from the figures below.
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
pengSummary <- penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(count = n(),
            median_bill_length_mm = median(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_body_mass_g = median(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))

pengSummary

  arrange(desc(bill_length_mm))

head(pengArr)

penguins_originalArr <- ggplot(data = pengArr, mapping = aes(x = bill_length_mm, 
                                                           y = body_mass_g,
                                                           colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +

title: Penguins Data R Analysis
text:
Findings
Using group_by and summarise, I found the count and the median ‘bill_length_mm’ and ‘body_mass_g’ for each species. ‘Gentoo’ had the highest median body mass at 5000 g, while ‘Adelie’ and ‘Chinstrap’ had the exact same median body mass of 3700 g. ‘Chinstrap’ had the longest median bill length at 49.6 mm, which is longer than ‘Gentoo’ even though ‘Gentoo’ is much heavier, so body mass and bill length do not increase together across species.
Using the dplyr arrange function, I arranged the column ‘bill_length_mm’ in descending order, but it had no effect on the figure. I used fct_reorder to reorder the species based on ‘body_mass_g’, which also had no effect on the figure, so I used fct_rev, which reversed the species order. This led to the figure changing, with ‘Gentoo’ being the first species in the legend and having a red plot colour now. The data points on the plot remained the same, but the colour of the points changed. This is because factor levels are ordered alphabetically by default, and we can see that changing levels impacts analysis and visualization.

title: Penguins Data Python Analysis
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER, released under a CC0 licence. The dataset was first published as an R package; I loaded it here with the palmerpenguins Python package (version 0.1.6), a port of that original.
This post is the same analysis as my R post, translated into Python with pandas and matplotlib.
Two of the penguins are missing their bill and body mass measurements.
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

penguins = load_penguins()
peng_summary = (
    penguins
    .groupby("species")
    .agg(
        count=("species", "size"),
        median_bill_length_mm=("bill_length_mm", "median"),
        median_body_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "median"),
    )
    .reset_index()
)

title: Penguins Data Python Analysis
text:
Findings
Using groupby and agg, I found the count and the median ‘bill_length_mm’ and ‘body_mass_g’ for each species. ‘Gentoo’ had the highest median body mass at 5000 g, while ‘Adelie’ and ‘Chinstrap’ had the exact same median body mass of 3700 g. ‘Chinstrap’ had the longest median bill length at 49.55 mm, which is longer than ‘Gentoo’ even though ‘Gentoo’ is much heavier, so body mass and bill length do not increase together across species. These are the same numbers I got in R, except that pandas printed 49.55 mm where R printed 49.6 mm, because R rounded the value for display.
Using the pandas sort_values function, I sorted the column ‘bill_length_mm’ in descending order, but it had no effect on the figure. Python does not have factor levels, so instead I made a list of the species ordered by median ‘body_mass_g’ and reversed it, which is what fct_reorder and fct_rev did in R, and it gave the same order of ‘Gentoo’, ‘Chinstrap’, ‘Adelie’. I then looped through the species in that order. This led to the figure changing, with ‘Gentoo’ being the first species in the legend and having a blue plot colour now, and ‘Adelie’ changing from blue to green. The data points on the plot remained the same, but the colour of the points changed. This is because matplotlib assigns its colours in the order the species are plotted, and we can see that changing the order impacts analysis and visualization.

title: About
text:
Why data science
My best friend, who I met on my first day at SFU, is a data science major, so being around him introduced me to data science. I decided to take an introductory data science class in undergrad, and the use of classifiers was so amazing to me, especially how one can use modelling to predict an outcome. I took further data science classes and really enjoyed them, so I decided to pursue the Master of Data Science program at UBC.

title: About
text:
Outside of data science
My favourite hobbies are playing and watching sports, specifically playing cricket and basketball. I play on a cricket team that runs during the summer, and last year I had the third most runs in the division. I also love listening to music and going to concerts. My favourite artist is Drake, and I have gone to several concerts for artists such as Drake, The Weeknd, J. Cole, Lil Tecca, PartyNextDoor, and Bryson Tiller. My favourite cuisine is Indian food, but I’m always open to trying new food spots. On the weekend, I usually meet up with a friend and either play cricket and get food or go for a run.
